name: Jehovah's Witnesses
info: Jehovah's Witnesses are a nontrinitarian, millenarian and restorationist Christian denomination that grew from the Bible Student movement begun in Pittsburgh in 1870, known for door-to-door evangelism and for refusing military service and blood transfusions.

facts.origin: The United States: a Bible study group formed by Charles Taze Russell and others in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in 1870, which became the Bible Student movement; the name Jehovah's witnesses was adopted in 1931.
facts.founder: Charles Taze Russell, who co-founded Zion's Watch Tower Tract Society in 1881; Joseph Franklin Rutherford, who kept control of the Society after Russell's death and adopted the name in 1931.
facts.scriptures: The Protestant canon of the Bible, held to be inspired and inerrant, read in their own New World Translation of the Holy Scriptures (full version 1961); doctrine is stated through Watch Tower Society publications such as The Watchtower and Awake!
facts.followers: About 9.2 million members worldwide reported in 2025, with about 9 million publishers in about 119,500 congregations; independent demographic studies suggest only about half of those who identify as Witnesses are counted as active by the faith itself.

t: Jehovah's Witnesses believe that Jehovah is the only true god and not part of a Trinity, that Jesus is God's first creation, and that Armageddon is imminent and will be followed by an earthly paradise.

The movement grew from Charles Taze Russell's Bible Students, and under Joseph Rutherford adopted the name Jehovah's witnesses in 1931, introduced door-to-door preaching and moved to a centrally directed organisation.

Witnesses refuse military service, saluting flags and blood transfusions of whole blood; they were persecuted in Nazi Germany, where about 2,000 were sent to concentration camps, and are banned or restricted in some countries today.
dyk: In 1912 Charles Taze Russell was the most distributed Christian author in the United States, and in 2010 The Watchtower and Awake! were the world's most widely distributed magazines.
ev: Charles Taze Russell and others form a Bible study group in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
Zion's Watch Tower Tract Society is co-founded to organise and print the movement's publications
Joseph Franklin Rutherford is elected president of the Society in a disputed election, and tens of thousands leave in the following years
At a convention in Columbus, Ohio, Rutherford introduces the name Jehovah's witnesses
About 20,000 Witnesses live in Nazi Germany, and about 10,000 of them are imprisoned over the following years
The full New World Translation of the Holy Scriptures is released
After publications built expectation that Christ's thousand-year reign might begin, a failed prediction is followed by a decline in membership
Authority for doctrinal and organisational decisions passes from the Society's president to the Governing Body

sections.origins:
Jehovah's Witnesses are a nontrinitarian, millenarian and restorationist Christian denomination that grew out of the Bible Student movement of the nineteenth century. In 1870 Charles Taze Russell and others formed a group in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to study the Bible, and Russell came to dispute several tenets of mainstream Christianity, among them the immortality of the soul, hellfire, predestination and the Trinity. In 1876 he met Nelson H. Barbour, and that year they produced the book Three Worlds, which taught that Jesus had begun the "harvest of the Gospel age" by an invisible return in 1874 and that 1914 would end a 2,520-year period called "the Gentile Times". The two split over doctrine in June 1879, and in July Russell began publishing Zion's Watch Tower and Herald of Christ's Presence.

From 1879 Watch Tower supporters gathered as autonomous congregations, and thirty were founded. Zion's Watch Tower Tract Society was co-founded in 1881 and incorporated in 1884 as a nonprofit business to distribute tracts and Bibles. Russell moved its headquarters to Brooklyn, New York City, in 1909 and identified the movement as the Bible Students. By 1910 about 50,000 people worldwide were associated with it. He died on 31 October 1916, aged 64.
sections.beliefs:
Jehovah's Witnesses believe that Jehovah, the form of God's name they prefer, is the only true god and the creator of all things, and that he is not part of a Trinity. They hold that Jesus is God's only direct creation and his "only-begotten Son", the first angel, who died on a single upright post rather than a cross, and that the Holy Spirit is God's applied power or "active force". They believe death is a state of nonexistence, reject a hell of fiery torment, and hold that a "little flock" of 144,000 will go to heaven to rule with Jesus while the majority are resurrected to a cleansed earth after Armageddon.

They believe that Jesus began to rule invisibly in heaven as king in October 1914, that the present world system will soon be destroyed at Armageddon, and that the earth will then become a paradise. They regard all other religions as false, identifying them with Babylon the Great, and consider human governments to be controlled by Satan. They do not observe Christmas, Easter, birthdays or other holidays and customs they consider to have pagan origins. They are told to reject the transfusion of whole blood, a prohibition that has existed since 1945, based on their reading of Acts 15:28, 29.

Worship takes place at Kingdom Halls, which contain no religious symbols, and since 2009 congregations meet twice a week. The Memorial of Christ's death, on the fourteenth day of the Jewish month Nisan, is the most important annual event, and only those who consider themselves anointed partake of the bread and wine.
sections.texts:
Jehovah's Witnesses consider the entire Protestant canon the inspired, inerrant word of God, interpret much of it literally while accepting parts as symbolic, and are old Earth creationists. They prefer their own translation, the New World Translation of the Holy Scriptures, which Nathan Knorr commissioned and which was released in full in 1961. Bible scholars including Bruce M. Metzger and MacLean Gilmour have said that scholarship is evident in it but that its rendering of certain texts is inaccurate and biased in favour of Witness practices and doctrines; other critics call it scholastically dishonest. Most of the criticism concerns the New Testament, especially the introduction of the name Jehovah and passages related to the Trinity.

The movement's teaching has come largely through periodicals and books. Russell published a six-book series, Studies in the Scriptures, and by 1912 was the most distributed Christian author in the United States. In 1917 Rutherford released The Finished Mystery as a seventh volume, which he claimed to be Russell's posthumous work but which Clayton Woodworth, George Fisher and Gertrude Seibert had written. In 2010 The Watchtower and Awake! were the world's most widely distributed magazines, and the group's website jw.org replaced watchtower.org in 2008.

The Governing Body issues no single statement of faith and states its positions through Watch Tower Society publications, which teach that doctrinal changes come through "progressive revelation" and "new light". Members are discouraged from reaching "private ideas" through Bible research independent of these publications.
sections.spread:
Under Russell the movement grew from the thirty congregations of 1879 and 1880. By about 1900 he had organised thousands of part- and full-time colporteurs, was appointing foreign missionaries and establishing branch offices, and by the 1910s his organisation kept nearly a hundred "pilgrims", or travelling preachers. About 50,000 people worldwide were associated with the movement by 1910.

Under Rutherford tens of thousands of defections occurred in the first half of his tenure, leading to several independent Bible Student organisations, the largest of which was the Dawn Bible Students Association. By mid-1919 an estimated one in seven of Russell-era Bible Students had ceased their association with the Society, and between 1921 and 1931 three-quarters were estimated to have left, although Alan Rogerson believes the total number to be unclear. Under Knorr, who became president in 1942, international assemblies, training programmes, missionary activity and branch offices expanded worldwide.

From 1966 publications and convention talks built anticipation that Jesus' thousand-year reign might begin in 1975 or shortly thereafter. Baptisms rose from about 59,000 in 1966 to more than 297,000 in 1974, and by 1975 the number of active members exceeded two million. Membership declined significantly for a few years after the prediction failed. In 2025 Jehovah's Witnesses reported about 9 million publishers in about 119,500 congregations and a worldwide annual increase of 2.5%.
sections.community:
Jehovah's Witnesses are organised hierarchically in what the leadership calls a theocratic organisation, directed by the Governing Body, an all-male group that establishes all doctrines. Branch offices, each also called Bethel, manage activities in countries or regions, and volunteers called Bethelites live and work there. Each congregation has unpaid male elders and ministerial servants appointed under a traveling overseer; the denomination does not use elder as a title for a formal clergy-laity division. Only men may hold positions of authority. Funding is largely donated by members, with no tithing or collection.

Members are expected to preach, often in pairs, and to submit a monthly report; those who do not report for six consecutive months are termed "inactive". Baptism, which they consider required for salvation, is not practised on infants. Members who commit serious offences may be expelled and shunned, and so are those who formally leave, who are termed "disassociated". Most limit their social interaction with non-Witnesses, whom they regard as living in a world influenced by Satan.

The denomination has been variously described as a church, sect, new religious movement or cult, and academics generally stopped using the term cult in the 1980s because of its pejorative associations. Alan Rogerson describes the leadership as totalitarian, which James Irvin Lichti rejects. A 2008 US Pew Forum survey found that about 37% of people raised in the group continued to identify as Jehovah's Witnesses, and that 65% of adult American Witnesses are converts.
sections.legacy:
The refusal of military service and of saluting flags and anthems has brought the group into conflict with several governments. In 1918 Watch Tower Society directors were jailed for sedition under the Espionage Act after The Finished Mystery criticised clergy and Christian involvement in the Great War, and members were subjected to mob violence; the directors were released in March 1919 and the charges dropped in 1920. In 1933 there were approximately 20,000 Witnesses in Nazi Germany, of whom about 10,000 were imprisoned. About 2,000 were sent to concentration camps, where they were identified by purple triangles, and as many as 1,200 died, including 250 who were executed. Unlike Jews and Romani, who were persecuted for their ethnicity, Witnesses could escape persecution by signing a document renouncing their faith.

Their activities are banned or restricted in some countries, including China, Russia, Vietnam and many Muslim-majority countries, and members have been imprisoned for refusing conscription. Their legal challenges have influenced civil rights legislation in several countries.

The group has also drawn criticism for unfulfilled predictions about 1914, 1925 and 1975. Norway ended its state funding of the community because of its shunning policy, concluding that shunning, particularly of children, constitutes psychological violence. Its policies on child sexual abuse have been examined in inquiries, including Australia's Royal Commission in 2015 and an inquiry by the Charity Commission for England and Wales begun in 2017; the organisation maintains that the best way to protect children is to educate parents.

summary: Jehovah's Witnesses are a nontrinitarian Christian denomination that grew from Charles Taze Russell's Bible Students and took its name in 1931 under Joseph Rutherford. Known for evangelism, refusal of military service and of whole-blood transfusions, they reported about 9.2 million members in 2025 and were persecuted in Nazi Germany.
references: George D. Chryssides, Jehovah's Witnesses: Continuity and Change (Ashgate Publishing, 2016)
Andrew Holden, Jehovah's Witnesses: Portrait of a Contemporary Religious Movement (Routledge, 2002)
Zoe Knox, Jehovah's Witnesses and the Secular World: From the 1870s to the Present (Palgrave Macmillan, 2018)
M. James Penton, Apocalypse Delayed: The Story of Jehovah's Witnesses (University of Toronto Press, 1997)
notes: Start is 1870, the Pittsburgh Bible study group; the article calls the movement 'founded by Charles Taze Russell in the nineteenth century' and gives 1881 for the Society and 1931 for the name.

The article's blood-transfusion paragraph carries two policy revisions dated 2026 (20 March and 18 September). The profile says only that members are told to reject whole blood, which holds on either reading; the 1945 date and 1961 expulsion are the article's.

Left out: the Pew 2016 income and diversity figures, the long sexual-abuse section's detail (figures of settlements, fines, the CBC investigation, the Silentlambs claims), gender and dating rules, 'PIMO', and the sociologists' typologies (Wilson, Beckford, Stark, Holden), as beyond the sections' room.

Whether Witnesses are Christians: the article calls the group a Christian denomination and gives only the Witnesses' own view that other denominations are false; it reports no outside dispute, so none is stated.

The article names 1914, 1925 and 1975 as past predictions; 1925 is the resurrection of the patriarchs announced in 1920. Membership: 'about 9.2 million' is the lede's figure; the Demographics section gives about 9 million publishers.

Faith map: years for areas other than the origin are the article's (1909 move, 1912 US author) or marked as the nearest the article gives; Warwick is from 'plans to completely move its operations to Warwick in 2017'. Coordinates of Warwick and Columbus are from general geography.
